Pope Paul VI: Head of the Catholic Church from 1963 to 1978.

She served as France's Minister of Justice under Sarkozy before later becoming Minister of Culture across four different governments, and has been mayor of one of Paris's arrondissements since 2008. Who is this French politician?

This short-lived 1990s state in the Balkans seceded from a disintegrating Yugoslavia in 1992, triggering a three-year war as rival Serb and Croat factions carved out their own unrecognized quasi-states — what state?
Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina: Balkan country (1992–1995)

A vocal critic of the Federal Reserve and mass surveillance programs, this Texas congressman ran for president as the Libertarian nominee in 1988 before seeking the Republican nomination twice more — who is he?
In Buddhism it caps the Noble Eightfold Path, and in the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali it's the eighth and final limb of Ashtanga Yoga — what meditative state is this?
Samadhi: State of meditative consciousness. Samādhi (Pali and Sanskrit: समाधि), in the Indian religions, is a state of meditative consciousness.
Co-leading a pro-Kurdish party to double-digit vote shares in Turkey's 2015 elections, this politician ran for president from behind bars in 2018 after his 2016 imprisonment — who is he?
Selahattin Demirtaş: Turkish politician. Selahattin Demirtaş (born 10 April 1973) is a Kurdish politician, lawyer and author.
Imprisoned and tortured as a young dissident under the Ottomans and once sentenced to death by the French, he went on to become the first president of independent Syria in 1943 — who was he?
This is the act of occupying an empty building or plot you don't own, rent, or have permission to use — often the seed of shanty towns in developing cities — what's it called?
Appointed by Emmanuel Macron in September 2025 after the previous government fell to a no-confidence vote, this politician had previously served as France's minister of the armed forces — who is he?
Sébastien Lecornu: Prime Minister of France since 2025.

Ruling the Ostrogothic Kingdom of Italy from 493 to 526 and later regent of the Visigoths too, this king received the old Western imperial regalia from Constantinople and was addressed by Italy's aristocracy as princeps. Who was he?
Theodoric the Great: King of Italy from 493 to 526. As ruler of the combined Gothic realms, Theodoric controlled an empire stretching from the Atlantic Ocean to the Adriatic Sea.
Hailed by the Senate as "the best ruler" and counted among the Five Good Emperors, this Hispania-born soldier pushed Rome to its greatest-ever territorial extent. Which emperor?
Trajan: Roman emperor from AD 98 to 117.
This philosophy and practice rejects treating animals as commodities, leading its followers to abstain from all animal-derived food, clothing, and entertainment. What is it?
This Warring States-era Chinese general commanded conquests of three rival kingdoms and is remembered by tradition as one of the four greatest generals of the late Warring States period — who was he?
Wang Jian (Qin): 3rd century BC Chinese military general.
Famous for pioneering sensationalist 'yellow journalism,' this publisher fought a fierce circulation war against Joseph Pulitzer's New York paper after acquiring a rival New York daily — who was he?
William Randolph Hearst: American newspaper publisher (1863–1951)
A former Palmach commando, this Israeli general became the first prime minister born in the region of Palestine — and was assassinated while serving a second term in 1995. Who was he?
Yitzhak Rabin: Prime Minister of Israel (1974–1977; 1992–1995)
A dispute between two rival lords escalated into a decade-long Japanese civil war from 1467 to 1477 that triggered the Warring States period — what was this conflict called?
Ōnin War: 15th-century civil war in Japan.
Who among these four was born earliest?
Ada Lovelace (born 1815) is the earliest of the four. Lovelace is often considered the first computer programmer.
Who among these was born first?
Benjamin Banneker (born 1731) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below was born first?
Eratosthenes (born 276 BC) is the earliest of the four.
Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four appeared earliest?
TeX (published 1978) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four is a physicist?
Ernest Lawrence is a physicist. A graduate of the University of South Dakota and University of Minnesota, Lawrence obtained a PhD in physics at Yale in 1925.
Pick the chemist from these four.
What is the atomic number of Helium?
Helium: Helium (from Ancient Greek: ἥλιος, romanized: helios, lit. 'sun') is a chemical element; it has symbol He and atomic number 2.
In what year was John Forbes Nash Jr. born?
John Forbes Nash Jr.: Nash and fellow game theorists John Harsanyi and Reinhard Selten were awarded the 1994 Nobel Prize in Economics.
In what year was Gabe Newell born?
Gabe Newell: Gabe Logan Newell (born November 3, 1962), also known by his nickname GabeN, is an American video game developer and businessman.
In what year was Carl Friedrich Gauss born?
Carl Friedrich Gauss: Gauss was director of the Göttingen Observatory in Germany and professor of astronomy from 1807 until his death in 1855.
In what year did Maria Montessori die?
Maria Montessori: At an early age, Montessori enrolled in classes at an all-boys technical school, with hopes of becoming an engineer.
In what year did Hedy Lamarr die?
Hedy Lamarr (born Hedwig Eva Maria Kiesler; November 9, 1914 – January 19, 2000) was an Austrian and American actress and inventor.
In what year was HIV/AIDS discovered?
HIV/AIDS: The human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) is a retrovirus that attacks the immune system.
In what year was COVID-19 discovered?
COVID-19: Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) is a contagious disease caused by the coronavirus SARS-CoV-2.
Mannitol: Pfizer. Mannitol is a type of sugar alcohol used as a sweetener and medication.
In which country did the Junkers Ju 87 take place?
Junkers Ju 87: Germany. The Junkers Ju 87, popularly known as the "Stuka", is a German dive bomber and ground-attack aircraft.
Who is credited with discovering Tellurium?
Tellurium: Franz-Joseph Müller von Reichenstein. Tellurium is a chemical element; it has the symbol Te and atomic number 52.
Who is credited with discovering Einsteinium?
Einsteinium: Albert Ghiorso. Einsteinium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Es and atomic number 99 and is a member of the actinide series and the seventh transuranium element.
Who is credited with discovering Neon?
Neon: William Ramsay. Neon is a chemical element; it has the symbol Ne and the atomic number 10.
Affecting about 1 in 30,000 newborns, this inherited condition — also called rod monochromacy — brings color blindness, poor acuity, and a curious day-blindness. What is it?
Achromatopsia is a medical syndrome that exhibits symptoms relating to five conditions, most notably monochromacy.
With one stable isotope and the rank of 12th-most-abundant element in the universe, this lightweight metal carries atomic number 13 — what is it?
Aluminium (the Commonwealth and preferred IUPAC name) or aluminum (North American English) is a chemical element; it has symbol Al and atomic number 13.
Whether contracted through the skin, the lungs, or the gut, this Bacillus-driven infection can take up to two months to show symptoms — what is it?
Anthrax is an infection caused by the bacterium Bacillus anthracis or Bacillus cereus biovar anthracis.

Named for the Ancient Greek word for 'star' after its flower shape, this group of roughly 170 mostly Eurasian perennial plants is also known for its late-blooming 'Michaelmas daisies' — which plant group?
Aster (genus) is a genus of perennial flowering plants in the family Asteraceae.
Ranging from 1 to 5 meters tall and found across Europe, Asia, Africa and the Americas, this shrub genus's best-known species is the European type also called barberry — what genus is it?
Berberis is a large genus of deciduous and evergreen shrubs from 1-5 m (3+12-16+12 ft) tall, found throughout temperate and subtropical regions of the world (apart from Australia).
Unlike most elements, this one is made almost entirely by cosmic ray collisions rather than inside stars, making it rare despite its light atomic weight. What element is it (symbol B)?
Boron is a chemical element; it has symbol B and atomic number 5.
The very same compound that hardens eggshells, builds pearls, and forms the chalk on a classroom board can also be swallowed as an antacid to calm an upset stomach — what is it?
Calcium carbonate is a chemical compound with the chemical formula CaCO3.
This set of metabolic reactions oxidizes biological fuels using an electron acceptor like oxygen to produce ATP, the molecule that stores usable chemical energy in cells — what is it?

Cellular respiration is the process of oxidizing biological fuels using an inorganic electron acceptor, such as oxygen, to drive production of adenosine triphosphate (ATP), which stores chemical energy in a biologically accessible form.

An organic compound found naturally in citrus fruits with the formula C6H8O7, over two million tons are manufactured annually for use as an acidifier, flavoring, and preservative. What is this compound?
Citric acid is an organic compound with the formula C6H8O7. In biochemistry, it is an intermediate in the citric acid cycle, which occurs in the metabolism of all aerobic organisms.
Lending its metal to sterling silver, cupronickel coins, and strain-gauge alloys, this element carries atomic number 29 and a name drawn from the Latin 'cuprum' — what is it?
Copper is a chemical element; it has symbol Cu (from Latin cuprum) and atomic number 29.

He's the only person to have won BAFTAs in black-and-white, colour, high-definition, 3D and 4K — a broadcasting career that began way back in 1954 hosting Zoo Quest. Who is this English natural historian?
David Attenborough (born 8 May 1926) is an English broadcaster, natural historian, and writer.
What flying insect, of which about 3,000 species exist, is known for its large compound eyes, two pairs of transparent wings, and often iridescent, metallic body coloration?
Dragonfly is a flying insect belonging to the infraorder Anisoptera below the order Odonata.
Not a single disease but a syndrome of overall brain dysfunction with many possible causes, this term's Greek roots literally mean 'brain suffering' — what is it called?
Encephalopathy (from Ancient Greek (enkphalos) 'brain' and (pthos) 'suffering') is any disorder or disease of the brain, especially chronic degenerative conditions.
Equivalent to one coulomb per volt, this SI unit of electrical capacitance is named after a pioneering English physicist — name the unit?
Farad (symbol: F) is the unit of electrical capacitance, the ability of a body to store an electrical charge, in the International System of Units (SI), equivalent to 1 coulomb per volt (C/V).
Having led Renault, Sauber, and Alfa Romeo's F1 outfits, this French engineer took the reins at Ferrari as team principal in 2023 — who is he?
Fred Vasseur (French; born 28 May 1968) is a French motorsport executive, businessman and engineer.
This pancreatic hormone kicks in when blood sugar dips too low, prompting the liver to convert stored glycogen back into glucose. What is it?
Glucagon is a peptide hormone, produced by alpha cells of the pancreas.
The first Professor of the Public Understanding of Mathematics at Cambridge, she's also a BBC broadcaster who explores the math behind human relationships — who is she?
Hannah Fry (born 21 February 1984) is a British mathematician, author and broadcaster.
This small rodent, with a pointed snout and a long, nearly hairless tail, has thrived by living alongside humans to the point that truly wild populations are now rare — what animal is it?
House mouse (Mus musculus) is a small mammal of the rodent family Muridae, characteristically having a pointed snout, large rounded ears, and a long and almost hairless tail.
Equal to one-twelfth of a foot and derived from the Roman word for 'twelfth,' this unit of length is often understood as roughly the width of a human thumb — name the unit?
Inch (symbol: in or) is a unit of length in the British Imperial and the United States customary systems of measurement.

This Swiss psychologist's theory of cognitive development, paired with his epistemological views, is together known as genetic epistemology, and remains foundational in early-childhood education. Who is he?
Jean Piaget (9 August 1896 - 16 September 1980) was a Swiss psychologist known for his work on child development.
Arrested in 1995 for various computer crimes and imprisoned for five years, this convicted hacker later became a computer-security consultant and author — who is he?
Kevin Mitnick (August 6, 1963 - July 16, 2023) was an American computer security consultant, author, and convicted hacker.
Distinguished from its cousins the pikas by short furry tails and elongated ears and hind legs, this mammal family comprises over 70 species we commonly call rabbits and hares — which family?
Leporidae is the family of rabbits and hares (Lepus), containing over 70 species of extant mammals in all.
Serving under Chancellor Adenauer, this economist championed West Germany's postwar economic miracle before becoming chancellor himself in 1963 — who is he?
Ludwig Erhard (4 February 1897 - 5 May 1977) was a German politician and economist who served as the second chancellor of West Germany from 1963 until 1966.
Covering everything from B2B deals to a government's 'Got Milk?'-style campaigns, this business pillar means acquiring, satisfying and retaining customers — what is this discipline called?
Marketing is the act of acquiring, satisfying and retaining customers. It is one of the primary components of business management and commerce.
Connecting the diencephalon and cerebrum to the pons, this brainstem structure plays a role in vision, hearing, and staying alert -- what is it called?
Midbrain is the uppermost portion of the brainstem connecting the diencephalon and cerebrum with the pons.
This semiaquatic rodent can stay submerged for up to seventeen minutes, propelled mainly by its webbed hind feet while its long, scaly tail helps steer — what animal is it?
Muskrat (Ondatra zibethicus) is a medium-sized semiaquatic rodent.
First isolated by Scottish physician Daniel Rutherford, which group-15 nonmetal with atomic number 7 is the most abundant species in Earth's atmosphere?
Nitrogen is a chemical element; it has symbol N and atomic number 7.
Known for causing bones that fracture easily, this group of genetic disorders can also produce blue-tinted eye whites, short stature, and hearing loss. Name the condition?
Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI), colloquially known as brittle bone disease, is a group of genetic disorders that all result in bones that break easily.
Sometimes mistaken for wild pigs, these New World ungulates roam from the southwestern U.S. through Central and South America and into Trinidad — name the family?
Peccary (also javelinas or skunk pigs) are pig-like ungulates of the family Tayassuidae (New World pigs).

This subdiscipline of biology examines how organisms, organs, cells, and biomolecules carry out their chemical and physical functions, and its name derives from Greek words for 'nature' and 'study of' — what is it?
Physiology (from Ancient Greek (phsis) 'nature, origin' and - (-loga) 'study of') is the scientific study of functions and mechanisms in a living system.
A colorless salt that looks deceptively like sugar and dissolves easily in water, this compound is mostly used in gold mining — but a 200-to-300-milligram dose will kill nearly any human. What is it?
Potassium cyanide is a compound with the formula KCN.

Found across Africa, Asia, and Australia, this family of nonvenomous snakes includes some of the world's largest and kills by coiling to suffocate rather than by injecting venom — what is the family called?

Pythonidae are a family of nonvenomous snakes found in Africa, Asia, and Australia. The taxonomy of pythons has evolved, and they are now known to be more closely related to sunbeam snakes and the Mexican burrowing python.

A brilliant English anatomist who coined the word 'Dinosauria,' meaning roughly 'terrible reptile,' he accepted that evolution happened but was an outspoken critic of Darwin's account of it. Who was he?
Richard Owen (20 July 1804 - 18 December 1892) was an English biologist, comparative anatomist and palaeontologist.
Nicknamed the seven-year itch, this contagious skin condition is caused by a microscopic burrowing mite and thrives in crowded places like prisons and care homes — what is it?
Scabies (also sometimes known as the seven-year itch) is a contagious human skin infestation by the tiny (0.2-0.45 mm) mite Sarcoptes scabiei, variety hominis.

Built for the Marine Corps by adding a third engine and a seventh main rotor blade to an earlier heavy-lift helicopter, this aircraft entered service in 1981 and flies from Navy ships — which helicopter?
Sikorsky CH-53E Super Stallion is a heavy lift helicopter operated by the United States military.
Doctors examine the color of this coughed-up airway mucus — greenish or yellow tints can hint at infection, though not which organism caused it — what is it?
Sputum is mucus that is coughed up from the lower airways (the trachea and bronchi).

Caused by the spiral bacterium Treponema pallidum, this infection famously announces itself with a single painless ulcer called a chancre, then a rash that loves the palms and soles — which sexually transmitted disease is it?

Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum subspecies pallidum. The signs and symptoms depend on the stage it presents: primary, secondary, latent or tertiary.

Beloved by biologists for its wild morphological variation and elaborate nest-building, this northern fish tolerates big swings in salinity, living in the sea but breeding in fresh water — what is it?
Three-spined stickleback (Gasterosteus aculeatus) is a fish native to most inland and coastal waters north of 30N.

It spawned a maritime patrol version (the Tu-142) and even a passenger airliner (the Tu-114), and Russia expects to keep flying this propeller-driven bomber until at least 2040 — which aircraft is it?
Tupolev Tu-95 (NATO reporting name: "Bear") is a Soviet nuclear-capable large, four-engine turboprop strategic bomber and missile platform.

Belonging to the same family as kangaroos, this informally named group of smaller macropods is native to Australia and New Guinea, with introduced populations as far away as Hawaii and the UK — what are they called?
Wallaby is a small or middle-sized macropod native to Australia and New Guinea, with introduced populations in New Zealand, Hawaii, the United Kingdom and other countries.
Also called humped cattle for the fatty growth on its shoulders, this South Asian breed group is used for everything from plowing to dairy, and even kept as pets in miniature form — what is it?
Zebu (Bos indicus), also known as indicine cattle and humped cattle, is a species or subspecies of domestic cattle originating in South Asia.

Typically affecting women between 35 and 50, this uterine condition occurs when endometrial-like tissue grows within the muscular wall of the uterus, causing painful, heavy periods — what is it called?
Adenomyosis: Extension of endometrial tissue into the myometrium.
On 18 March 1965, this Soviet cosmonaut became the first person to walk in space, spending over twelve minutes outside his capsule during a Voskhod mission — who is he?

Capable of constantly changing its shape by extending and retracting temporary 'false feet,' this single-celled organism turns up across nearly every branch of the eukaryotic tree of life — what is it?
Shed and regrown every year on most male deer, this bony head growth serves as both a weapon and a symbol of sexual attraction — what is it?
Antler: Skull projections found in deer.

This umbrella term for joint disease covers conditions like osteoarthritis, most common in weight-bearing joints as people age, and the autoimmune form that typically targets the hands and feet. What condition is this?
This Indian jurist studied economics at Columbia and the London School of Economics before becoming the chief architect of his country's constitution. Who was he?
B. R. Ambedkar: Indian jurist, economist, politician and social reformer (1891–1956)
One of the richest people alive, this French chairman and CEO turned his father's construction firm toward real estate before building the world's largest luxury-goods empire — who is he?
Credited with kicking off the Jet Age, this swept-wing quadjet airliner entered regular passenger service with Pan Am in October 1958 — which aircraft?

Best known for his role as Ben Hunter in a soapy prime-time revenge drama, this American actor also starred as Will Davis on The CW's 'Privileged' and Kyle Parks on Lifetime's 'The Client List.' Who is he?
Formed when quicklime reacts with water, this compound goes by names like slaked lime and builders' lime, and is used in food prep under the additive code E526 — what is it?
Calcium hydroxide: Inorganic compound of formula Ca(OH)2.

This American Nobel laureate coined the term 'bioorthogonal chemistry' for reactions that work inside living systems, building chemical tools to study the cell-surface sugars called glycans. Who is she?
Despite no clinical evidence it treats any disease, this daisy-like herb is brewed into calming teas and can trigger uterine contractions in its Roman variety — what is it?
Chamomile: Common name for several daisy-like plants.
In this chronic liver condition, healthy tissue is replaced by scar tissue and regenerative nodules, choking blood flow and causing portal hypertension — what is it called?
Cirrhosis: Chronic disease of the liver, characterized by fibrosis.

Nicknamed 'flying lemurs' despite not being lemurs at all, these Southeast Asian gliding mammals are primates' closest living relatives and belong to an order whose name means 'skin wing' — what are they called?
Its round nuts distinguish it from the longer filbert, and its coppiced wood once built wattle-and-daub walls across England — which shrub?
Corylus avellana: Species of tree (common hazel)
Two polynucleotide chains coil around each other into a double helix to carry the genetic instructions of nearly every living thing — what is this macromolecule?
DNA: Molecule that carries genetic information.
Sold under the brand name Valium, this benzodiazepine anxiolytic treats anxiety, seizures, alcohol withdrawal, and muscle spasms — and can even induce memory loss during procedures; what is it?
Diazepam: Benzodiazepine sedative. Diazepam, sold under the brand name Valium among others, is a medication of the benzodiazepine family that acts as an anxiolytic.
The only living relative of the extinct Steller's sea cow, this seagrass-grazing marine mammal is most abundant in the waters of northern Australia — what is it?
Dugong: Species of marine mammal. It is one of four living species of the order Sirenia, which also includes three species of manatees.
The first woman admitted to MIT, this environmental chemist was the first to apply chemistry to nutrition and founded the home economics movement — who was she?
Ellen Swallow Richards: American engineer and chemist (1843–1911)
The major female sex hormone, this estrogen drives the development of secondary sexual characteristics and helps maintain reproductive tissues from puberty through pregnancy — what is it?

Recognized by their pod-like fruit and compound leaves, this plant family — the third-largest among flowering plants — includes beans, peas, and lentils along with genera like Acacia and Mimosa. What family is it?
Fabaceae: Family of legume flowering plants. Fabaceae or Leguminosae, commonly known as the legume, pea, or bean family, is a large and agriculturally important family of flowering plants.
This whip-like appendage propels sperm cells and lets bacteria like Helicobacter pylori swim through stomach mucus, sometimes triggering ulcers — what is it called?
Flagellum: Cellular appendage functioning as locomotive or sensory organelle.

Unlike plants, this kingdom of life can't photosynthesize, and unlike most things, it has chitin in its cell walls — feeding instead by oozing digestive enzymes out and absorbing what dissolves. What group includes yeasts, molds, and mushrooms?
Fungus: Organism belonging to kingdom Fungi.
Recognized as the world's longest ray-finned fish, this ribbon-shaped, silvery-blue deep-sea creature is often blamed for sea-serpent legends — which fish?
Giant oarfish: Species of oceanic ray-finned fish.
Descended from medieval hunting dogs once used to take down bears, boar, and deer for German nobility, this breed ties with the Irish Wolfhound as one of the world's two largest — which breed is it?
Great Dane: German breed of dog. The Great Dane is a German breed of large mastiff-sighthound, which descends from hunting dogs of the Middle Ages used to hunt bears, wild boar, and deer.
This German-American physicist won a 1967 Nobel Prize for explaining how a nuclear cycle powers heavy stars, after heading the Theoretical Division at Los Alamos during World War II — who is he?
Found in trace amounts in modern gasoline blends, this colorless, six-carbon alkane boils at about 69°C and serves as a cheap, low-reactivity solvent — what is it?
A colorless gas that throws off white fumes the moment it meets moist air, it turns into a familiar strong acid once dissolved in water — which compound, formula HCl?
Hydrogen chloride: Chemical compound. Hydrogen chloride gas and hydrochloric acid are important in technology and industry.
Equal to one-twelfth of a foot and derived from the Roman word for 'twelfth,' this unit of length has been pegged to exactly 25.4 millimeters since the mid-20th century — what is it?
Inch: Unit of length. The inch (symbol: in or ″) is a unit of length in the British Imperial and the United States customary systems of measurement.

The New York Times once called him "the nation's most influential evangelical leader," yet he was never an ordained minister — instead this psychologist founded Focus on the Family and led it from 1977 to 2010. Who was he?
James Dobson: American evangelical Christian psychologist and author (1936–2025)
Struggling with a morphine addiction from a Civil War saber wound, this pharmacist and chemist developed a coca-and-caffeine beverage in 1886 that became Coca-Cola — who is he?
John Stith Pemberton: American pharmacist, inventor of Coca-Cola (1831–1888)
First described in 1845 by a German physicist, these two equalities govern current and voltage in electrical networks and generalized Georg Ohm's work — what are they called?
Kirchhoff's circuit laws: Two equalities that deal with the current and potential difference.
This biennial vegetable in the onion family has an edible bundle of leaf sheaths sometimes colloquially called a 'stem' — what is it?
Leek: Vegetable in the onion family. A leek is a biennial vegetable, a cultivar of Allium ampeloprasum, the broadleaf wild leek (syn.
Tucked mostly beneath the right rib cage, this organ detoxifies the body, stores glucose as glycogen, and produces the bile that helps digest fat — which organ?
Liver: Vertebrate organ involved in metabolism.
First synthesized in 1912 by a Merck chemist, this stimulant known on the street as ecstasy or molly became linked to raves and electronic dance music in the 1980s — which drug?
MDMA: Psychoactive drug, often called ecstasy.
Whether a milk board's 'Got Milk?' campaign or a city pitching itself as a tourist destination, this discipline boils down to acquiring, satisfying, and retaining customers — what is it?
Marketing: Study and process of exploring, creating, and delivering value to customers.
More than 80% of cases of this cancer — which grows in the thin lining covering the lungs and other organs — trace back to asbestos exposure. What is it?
With over 17,000 built and flown by more than 50 countries, this Soviet-designed twin-turbine machine is the most-produced helicopter in the world — what is it?
Mil Mi-8: Family of transport helicopters.
Its wings make an odd whistling sound on take-off, and one pair may raise up to six broods a year — which abundant North American gamebird?
Mourning dove: North American bird in the family Columbidae.
First identified from an 1856 fossil in a German valley, this group of archaic humans roamed Europe and Asia until vanishing around 40,000 years ago as modern humans arrived — who were they?

The first of the Century Series jet fighters, this supersonic aircraft was the U.S. Air Force's first fighter capable of level supersonic flight, first taking to the air in May 1953, seven months ahead of schedule — which jet?

North American F-100 Super Sabre: 1953 fighter aircraft family. The North American F-100 Super Sabre is an American supersonic jet fighter aircraft designed and produced by the aircraft manufacturer North American Aviation.
Named after an ancient Greek city, this cactus genus is better known by its fruit's common name, the prickly pear, and goes by nopal or sabra in other cultures — what genus is it?
Opuntia: Genus of cactus. The plant has been introduced to Australia, southern Europe, the Middle East, and parts of Africa.

Named after the bones that house them — frontal, maxillary, ethmoid, and sphenoid — these four paired air-filled spaces surround the nasal cavity and have a still-debated evolutionary purpose — what are they called?
Paranasal sinuses: Air-filled spaces surrounding the nasal cavity.
This inflammation of the sac surrounding the heart causes sharp chest pain that eases when sitting up and worsens when lying down or breathing deeply — what condition is it?
Pericarditis: Inflammation of the pericardium. Pericarditis (PER-i-kar-DYE-tis) is inflammation of the pericardium, the fibrous sac surrounding the heart.
Their name blends the Greek for "plant" and "drifter": these self-feeding plankton photosynthesize in the sunlit surface waters of oceans and lakes — what are they?
Phytoplankton: Autotrophic members of the plankton ecosystem.
Native to Southeast Asia and tasting like a sweet grapefruit, this non-hybrid citrus is the largest of them all — in fact, an ancestor of both the grapefruit and the bitter orange — what is it?
Pomelo: Citrus fruit from Southeast Asia.
Created in the early 18th century, this dark pigment was the first modern synthetic color, made by oxidizing iron ferrocyanide salts — what is it?
Prussian blue: Synthetic pigment. Prussian blue (also known as Berlin blue, Brandenburg blue, Parisian and Paris blue) is a dark blue pigment produced by oxidation of ferrous ferrocyanide salts.
Element 88 reacts with nitrogen rather than oxygen in air, turning black, and once glowed in self-luminous paints despite being highly carcinogenic — which element is it?
Radium: Chemical element with atomic number 88 (Ra)

Grown for its fleshy, edible stalks since before the 18th century in Europe and Scandinavia, this plant's broad triangular leaves are actually poisonous due to their high oxalic acid content. What is it?
Rhubarb: Species of herbaceous perennial plant with fleshy, sour edible stalks.
First identified in November 2002 and traced through civets to horseshoe bats in Yunnan, this viral respiratory disease had an 11% fatality rate before its outbreak ended in 2003 — which disease?
Creator of a satirical comic strip about corporate cubicle life, this cartoonist also wrote the pandeistic novella 'God's Debris' — who is he?
Scott Adams: American cartoonist and author (1957–2026)
This crustacean typically swims forward using its swimmerets but can flick its tail to dart backward in a defensive move called 'lobstering' — what is it?
Also called the mountain-ash despite not being a true ash, this rose-family tree grows small red berries beloved by birds — which species?
Sorbus aucuparia: Species of flowering plant in the rose family Rosaceae.
Whose pure-white winter coat became 'ermine,' the prized fur trimming the ceremonial robes of the UK House of Lords — and which was disastrously introduced to New Zealand? What animal is it?
Sometimes called gadflies, the females of this fly family bite land animals, including humans, to get the blood protein they need to produce eggs — which family?
Tabanidae: Family of insects. Horse flies and deer flies are true flies in the family Tabanidae in the insect order Diptera.
Encompassing everything from storytelling to painting, this broad domain of human creative expression splits into three branches: visual, literary, and performing — what is it called?
The arts: Creative human and cultural expression. The arts, or creative arts, are a vast range of human practices involving creative expression, storytelling, and cultural participation.
Covered in taste buds and divided into oral and pharyngeal parts, this muscular mouth organ also helps clean the teeth and enable speech — what is it?
Tongue: Muscular organ in the mouth of most vertebrates.
Nicknamed the "immortal jellyfish," this tiny sea creature can revert from a sexually mature adult back into an immature, sea-floor-dwelling polyp stage instead of dying — what species is it?
Turritopsis dohrnii: Species of small, biologically immortal jellyfish.
Also called vervain, this genus of roughly 150 flowering plant species is native mostly to the Americas and Asia, though its European type species grows wild there too — what genus is it?
